Learning Objectives
Specify appropriate aspects of patient optimization before revision total knee arthroplasty.
Establish the role of various imaging modalities in planning for revision total knee arthroplasty.
Identify intraoperative needs with regard to implants and equipment for revision total knee
arthroplasty.
Overview
Revision total knee arthroplasty (TKA) is an increasingly important procedure in orthopaedics
because of growing patient volumes and associated costs.1
To ensure successful revision TKA, a systematic approach to surgical planning is required.

necessary intraoperative equipment and implants, and postoperative care may be helpful3

Patient Expectations
To ensure the success of any surgery, including revision TKA, patients must have appropriate
preoperative expectations.
The surgeon’s job is to distinguish appropriate expectations from patient desires.
Patient expectations are highly indicative of postoperative outcomes and satisfaction after
total joint arthroplasty.4
Patient satisfaction is lower 2 years after revision TKA compared with 2 years after primary
TKA.
Surgeons also should discuss increased complication rates and decreased survivorship
compared with primary TKA.5-7

Any successful surgical procedure, including revision TKA, requires that the patient has
appropriate expectations preoperatively. Surgeons must distinguish patient desires from
appropriate expectations. Mahomed et al4 reported that patient expectations are highly
indicative of outcomes and satisfaction after total joint arthroplasty. This is especially
important with regard to revision TKA because many patients do not realize that revision
TKA is associated with higher rates of complications, increased stiffness, and lower
functional levels than primary TKA. Studies have reported that patient satisfaction 2
years after revision TKA is lower compared with 2 years after primary TKA. Hartley et al8
reported that 83% of patients who underwent primary TKA were satisfied, whereas 66%
of patients who underwent revision TKA were satisfied.
Postoperative range of motion (ROM) is one outcome that should be discussed with
patients before revision surgery. Postoperative ROM may vary substantially, depending
on the reason for revision and the type of revision being performed. In general, patients
undergoing revision TKA have decreased postoperative ROM compared with individuals
undergoing primary TKA. One study attributed this diminished flexion to low
preoperative (<103°) and intraoperative flexion (<117°), young age (<44 years), and
constrained condylar and constrained prosthesis types.9 Conversely, after revision
surgery for stiffness, most patients have improved ROM; however, the literature is
inconsistent with regard to how much improvement can be expected postoperatively.10-
13
Discussions about increased complication rates and decreased survivorship with revision
TKA compared with primary TKA also are important.5-7 These differences are the result
of multiple factors, including scarring; diminished bone stock; decreased quality of bone
and soft tissue; potential ligamentous laxity; and, sometimes, a history of periprosthetic
joint infection. In addition, revision TKA may require more constrained components,
which place additional stress on fixation interfaces. In addition, patients in whom TKA
fails and in whom revision TKA is required may be less healthy than those undergoing
primary TKA or may be more prone to complications because of systemic health
conditions or anatomic factors. In addition, these patients are older and often are less
healthy than they were at the time of index TKA. Patients must be educated about these

Preoperative Optimization
All relevant modifiable risk factors should be addressed as best as possible before revision
TKA.
Optimize body mass index as much as possible, with a goal of less than 40 kg/m2. 
A hemoglobin A1c level of less than 7% to 8% 
Smoking cessation or decreased smoking for 4 to 6 weeks before and after surgery 
Nutritional optimization, with an albumin level higher than 3.5 g/dL
Urinary screen if symptoms of a urinary tract infection (UTI) are present. 
Optimization of surgical candidates must be weighed against the risk of delayed revision
surgery. 

Preoperative Optimization
Surgeons must address any modifiable risk factors as best as possible before performing
revision TKA. Similar to primary TKA, modifiable patient risk factors, including body mass
index, hemoglobin A1c levels, smoking, nutrition, and UTI, should be optimized, if
present. The ability to optimize a patient’s outcome depends on the urgency of revision.
The association between increasing body mass index and increased complication rates is
well established.14 Although not all patients may be able to achieve this, especially given
the urgency of revision surgery, a goal body mass index is less than 40 kg/m2. In
addition, many patients who are overweight may be malnourished. Because losing a
substantial amount of weight safely before a revision procedure may be difficult, the
focus should be on patient education and nutrition. No definitive hemoglobin A1c cutoff
level exists with regard to optimal surgical outcome; however, effective control of
diabetes mellitus may lead to more stable perioperative glucose levels and decreased
risk of perioperative complications. A general rule of thumb is a target hemoglobin A1c
level of less than 7% to 8%.15 Perioperative glucose control likely is equally or even more
important. Smoking has been shown to increase complications in patients undergoing

and patients should attempt to be tobacco free for 6 weeks before surgery. Routine
screening for a UTI also is controversial; however, perioperative UTI has been associated

In the revision setting, optimization of surgical candidates must be weighed against the
risk of delayed surgical treatment. Depending on the indication for revision TKA, a
substantial delay in surgery may result in negative outcomes, such as periprosthetic
fracture, extensor mechanism disruption, worsening bone loss, increased osteolysis,
damage to well-fixed components, and overall patient deconditioning, which may affect
postoperative rehabilitation (Figure 1).

Preoperative Laboratory Values
A full set of preoperative laboratory tests, including basic metabolic panel, complete blood
count, hemoglobin A1c levels, erythrocyte sedimentation rate/C-reactive protein (CRP) level,
and type and screen, typically are obtained before revision TKA. A few laboratory values
deserve special mention.
Laboratory values for infection (Figure 2)
Infection must be ruled out before revision joint replacement. The Musculoskeletal Infection
Society has established criteria for the diagnosis of periprosthetic joint infection.18
Useful screening laboratory studies for infection include erythrocyte sedimentation rate, CRP
level, and D-dimer.
Joint fluid should be aspirated if clinical concern for infection exists or if screening laboratory
studies are elevated.
Aspirate should be sent for culture (consider holding for 14 days), cell count, and differential.
Advanced tests, such as alpha-defensin, synovial CRP level, or polymerase chain reaction–
based tests, may be considered, particularly if aspiration is being repeated because of
equivocal results.
Obtaining intraoperative frozen pathology may be considered in patients with equivocal
results.

Preoperative Laboratory Values
A complete set of preoperative laboratory studies, including a basic metabolic panel (or
comprehensive metabolic panel), complete blood count, hemoglobin A1c level, and type
and screen, typically are obtained before primary and revision TKA; however, surgeons
always must rule out infection before revision joint replacement. The Musculoskeletal
Infection Society has established criteria for the diagnosis of periprosthetic joint
infection.18 Useful screening values for infection include erythrocyte sedimentation rate
(>30 mm/hr), CRP level (>10 mg/L), and D-dimer. These are nonspecific laboratory values
that may be elevated for various reasons. In addition, within 6 weeks of index surgery,
erythrocyte sedimentation rate is less useful and the CRP screening threshold is higher
(>100 mg/L).19 These values are not diagnostic of infection but indicate the need for
additional testing, typically in the form of joint aspiration.
Although some surgeons recommend routine preoperative aspiration in the revision
setting, joint fluid should definitely be obtained if clinical concern for infection exists or if
screening laboratory values are elevated. Aspirate should be sent for culture (consider
holding for 14 days), cell count, and differential. Advanced tests, such as a-defensin,
synovial CRP level, and polymerase chain reaction?based tests, may be considered,
particularly if aspiration will be repeated because of equivocal results. Intraoperative
frozen pathology sampling also should be considered if the diagnosis of infection is
unclear after the preoperative workup. The criterion for a positive test result usually is
set at greater than 5 to 10 neutrophils per high-powered field in five high-powered fields
at a of magnification ×400. Tissue should be sent from areas where neutrophils normally
are not present (ie, they are naturally found in bone marrow, blood, or the synovium of
patients with inflammatory arthritis).

Many patients undergoing revision TKA have anemia as a result of recent surgery,
chronic disease, or iron deficiency. Anemia is particularly common in patients being
treated for periprosthetic joint infection. These patients often have multiple
comorbidities and anemia of chronic disease, and their hemoglobin level may be low as
a result of recent joint replacement or explantation. Preoperative anemia is an
independently predictor of complications after revision total joint arthroplasty.20
Therefore, referral to a hematologist or primary care provider for medical management
of anemia and optimization before revision TKA may be considered in female patients
with a preoperative hemoglobin level of less than 12 g/dL and in male patients with a
hemoglobin level of less than 13 g/dL, depending on surgical history and underlying
diagnosis.21 Management of anemia may include correcting the underlying cause, iron
supplementation, nutritional supplementation, or other strategies. Starting hemoglobin
and/or hematocrit levels may predict the need for intraoperative blood transfusion.
Communication with the anesthesia team regarding blood loss is crucial. This is
particularly important in revision surgery, which often is lengthy and typically involves
patients with a low starting hemoglobin level.
Given the potential for blood transfusion, all patients undergoing revision TKA should
undergo type and screen testing to ensure that blood will be available as necessary.
Although this laboratory test may have been done on hospital admission, the result is
valid for only a limited time. Therefore, surgeons should verify that an updated, valid
type and screen has been performed.

Many studies have shown a considerable association between preoperative malnutrition and
complications in orthopaedic surgery.
Albumin level of less than 2.5 g/dL
Absolute lymphocyte count of less than 1,100 cells/mL
Dental evaluation
Considerable dental decay is associated with increased bacterial counts, which have been
implicated in the development of periprosthetic infection in published studies.

Vascular evaluation
All patients should be evaluated for peripheral pulses in the lower extremity.
Ankle brachial index or formal vascular evaluation if concerning venous insufficiency of the

Soft-tissue evaluation
Prior incisions must be identified, and the type of incision that will be used for revision
surgery should be determined. Patients with lower extremity lymphedema should undergo

Urologic issues
Foley catheters are used in many revision TKA procedures because of difficulty in predicting
the length of the procedure.
If a patient has urologic issues, the surgeon should assume that a Coudé catheter may be
necessary. In patients with severe benign prostatic hyperplasia or a history of difficult urinary
catheter insertion, a preoperative urology consultation may be warranted.
Anesthetic plan
Communication with the anesthesia team about the expected length of the procedure and
projected blood loss is important.
The anesthesiologist should be alerted before the procedure and before the stems are
cemented with pressurizing cement because of the risk of intraoperative hypotension.22

studies have shown a considerable association between preoperative malnutrition and
wound infections and other complications. Common screening laboratory studies

The utility of a preoperative dental evaluation is controversial. Considerable dental decay

undergone one in the past year is reasonable;3 however, surgeons may determine
whether a preoperative dental evaluation is required on a case-by-case basis. This is
especially pertinent if revision may be more urgent.
All patients should be evaluated for peripheral pulses and signs of vascular disease in
the lower extremity on physical examination. At a minimum, abnormal pulses—
particularly in patients with a history of atherosclerotic disease, vascular disease, or
other signs of arterial insufficiency—should prompt additional workup via noninvasive
vascular studies, such as the ankle-brachial index, or evaluation by a vascular surgeon. In
addition, venous insufficiency of the lower extremity should be noted because it
increases the risk of ulcers perioperatively, which should be discussed with the patient
preoperatively.
Physical examination also should include an examination of the soft tissues. Prior
incisions must be identified by the surgeon, and a determination must be made with
regard to which incision will be used for revision surgery. Patients with lower extremity
lymphedema should undergo aggressive preoperative treatment to minimize lower
extremity swelling, and referral to a lymphedema clinic may be considered
preoperatively to optimize the soft-tissue environment. Patients with prior flaps, skin
grafts, or scarred and non-pliable soft tissues can be referred to plastic surgery for help
with surgical exposure (Figure 3).

Review of Imaging Studies
Radiographs
Preoperative radiographs should be obtained for all patients undergoing revision joint
replacement.
Comparison of current radiographs with prior radiographs may be extremely helpful in
diagnosing the etiology of joint failure and is critical for preoperative planning.
Radiographs also aid in evaluating for potential bone defects, measuring the length of stems,
evaluating for prior hardware, and noting femoral or tibial deformity.
If possible, radiographs taken before index TKA should be obtained.
These radiographs may reveal the indication for index TKA, overall preoperative limb
alignment, the severity of arthritis, and bony anatomy, as well as the success of the index
procedure in achieving desired alignment, posterior condylar offset (PCO), and composite
patellar thickness.
Serial radiographs aid in documenting loosening.
Criteria for radiographic loosening include a wide or progressively enlarging radiolucency at
the cement-bone, metal-cement, or metal-bone interface; component migration or
subsidence; and cement fractures.24
Changes in implant position observed on serial images also may indicate component
loosening.

Osteolysis and relative stress shielding can be identified around the tibial implants.
Evaluation of implant size
Femoral and tibial sizes can be evaluated in the medial/lateral dimension based on
component overhang.
Can determine if subsidence of the tibial implant has occurred, particularly if compared
with prior radiographs.

Roentgen stereophotogrammetric analysis
Roentgen stereophotogrammetric analysis (RSA) generally is considered the most accurate
imaging modality for measuring prosthesis migration for TKA and total hip arthroplasty.
Despite being the most accurate imaging modality for measuring wear in TKA, RSA may be
impractical in most settings because of the high cost and limited access.

Review of Imaging Studies
Radiographs should be obtained before revision joint replacement in all patients
(Resource 2). Comparison with prior radiographs may be extremely helpful in diagnosing
the etiology of joint failure, and radiographs are critical for preoperative planning.
Radiographs are useful for evaluating potential bone defects, measuring the length of
stems, evaluating for prior hardware, and noting femoral or tibial deformity.
Radiographs from the index TKA procedure should be obtained whenever possible. This
allows for assessment of the indication for index TKA; overall preoperative limb
alignment; the severity of arthritis; bony anatomy; and the success of the procedure in
achieving desired alignment, PCO, and composite patellar thickness. Serial radiographs

Multiple radiographic views of the knee should be obtained for all patients. An AP view
aids in evaluating for osteolysis and stress shielding around both components; however,
these findings are better visualized on the tibial component on an AP view. Component
size in the medial/lateral dimension based on component overhang, and coronal
position and alignment can be evaluated. An AP view can be used to identify subsidence
of the tibial component, particularly if compared with prior radiographs. Polyethylene

Plan for New Implants
Before revision TKA, important considerations include the level of constraint necessary,
the type of stems necessary (cemented versus press fit), how bone defects will be filled,
and how fixation will be achieved (Video 3). The constraint of the knee prosthesis likely
will have to be increased by at least one level. To prepare, the surgeon should determine
what implants are kept in the operating room and what requests are necessary to have
them available for surgery. Typically, at least one additional level of constraint beyond
the preoperative plan should be available. Often, this level of constraint (eg, hinged
prosthesis) will need to be brought in specifically for the case. Prostheses that provide
varus/valgus constraint also should be available (Figures 12 and 13).
Having a plan for component fixation is essential. To guide this decision, surgeons
should determine how fixation will be achieved at the joint line, the metaphysis, and the
diaphysis. Planning for metaphyseal fixation and stems will ensure that all required
implants are available at the time of surgery. A nickel or cement (polymethyl
methacrylate) allergy is a unique patient consideration. The incidence of clinically
important allergy to these materials is a subject of debate but likely is very rare. If
concern for a nickel allergy exists, then nickel-free components, which are made of
hardened titanium or oxidized zirconium and are ceramic coated, should be available.
Although management of a suspected cement allergy is difficult in the revision setting,
fully press-fit revision components should be available.

Unless contraindicated, tranexamic acid should be part of the blood management plan
for all patients undergoing revision TKA. An increasing body of literature has shown that
the use of tranexamic acid in the revision TKA setting decreases the rate of blood
transfusions by as much as twofold without increasing the rate of venous
thromboembolism.38,39
In patients with anemia, consider using EPO. EPO acts on bone marrow to increase the
rate of red blood cell differentiation and maturation, increasing total red blood cell mass.
The use of preoperative EPO has been shown to be effective if a large amount of blood
loss was anticipated.35,36 EPO often is used under the direction of a hematologist or a
primary care provider (Table 4). Reinfusion systems may be considered, if available,
during revision procedures. Although evidence supporting the routine use of reinfusion
systems is inconsistent, they may be beneficial in the revision setting if a large amount of
blood loss is anticipated, particularly in patients who do not accept blood transfusions
for religious reasons.36

Postoperative protocols may depend on the details of the surgical procedure; however,
consideration of postoperative protocols preoperatively allows for management of patient
expectations, a discussion with the appropriate services, and ensures all equipment is

After revision TKA, typically a patient will be weight bearing as tolerated; however, in patients
in whom limited–weight bearing may be important, surgeons must discuss such
postoperative restrictions with the patient preoperatively because it may affect discharge
planning.
Weight bearing may be limited in patients with a fracture at the stem tip or if predominantly
cementless fixation is used with less robust bone.

Postoperative protocols may depend on the details of the procedure; however,
introducing a plan preoperatively helps manage patient expectations, facilitates
discussions with the appropriate services, and ensures that all equipment is available.
Typically, after revision TKA, a patient will be permitted to bear weight as tolerated;
however, surgeons should have a preoperative discussion with patients in whom
limited–weight bearing may be necessary postoperatively because it may affect
discharge planning. Limited–weight bearing may be necessary in patients with a fracture
at the stem tip and patients with less robust bone in whom predominantly noncemented
fixation is used. If surgical wound healing is a concern, then the short-term use (5 to 14
days) of a knee immobilizer may be considered. Strict elevation of the surgically
managed extremity also may be considered if concerns for postoperative swelling,
capsule integrity, or tension on the skin closure exist. A negative-pressure wound
dressing (incisional wound vac) may help promote wound healing.
A pain-control plan that is discussed with the patient preoperatively is important. Clearly,
the pain-control plan may change depending on the details of the surgery; however,
many patients in whom joint replacement fails already are being treated with pain
medications at the time of presentation to the orthopaedic clinic. The goal is that the
revision procedure will decrease the pain; however, patients often have some level of
physiologic and psychologic dependence on pain-control medications. A preoperative
discussion with the patient about the anticipated length of treatment with narcotics may
help avoid complications later in recovery.
The optimal prophylaxis for venous thromboembolism after revision TKA has not been
established, and whether more potent anticoagulation protocols are more effective or
necessary to prevent pulmonary embolism after revision TKA remains unclear.40,41

thromboembolism but also are associated with an increased risk for wound

undergoing revision TKA, discharge planning also is an important aspect of
